procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment upholding the preliminary objection raised on behalf of the Respondent and dismissing the election petition.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: An election petition (Election Petition No. 2 of 1985) was filed challenging the election of the respondent based on alleged corrupt practices. The respondent raised preliminary objections to the maintainability of the petition, arguing it lacked material facts and particulars and did not disclose a cause of action. The appellant filed two applications for amendment of the election petition (not to supply missing material facts). The High Court heard all applications together and dismissed the election petition.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court (Civil Appeal No. 2774 (NCE) of 1985). The Supreme Court was approached because the appellant challenged the validity of the High Court's view that an election petition lacking material facts and particulars of alleged corrupt practices and not disclosing a cause of action must be summarily dismissed. The appellant also argued that the High Court erred in dismissing the petition under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure instead of rejecting it.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was right in holding that an election petition must be summarily dismissed when the material facts and particulars of the alleged corrupt practices are not furnished and the petition does not disclose a cause of action.

facts: An elector (appellant) filed an election petition challenging the election of the returned candidate (respondent) on the grounds of alleged corrupt practices.

The respondent, instead of filing a written statement, raised a preliminary objection that the petition lacked the necessary material facts and particulars and therefore did not disclose a cause of action.
The High Court agreed with the respondent's preliminary objection and summarily dismissed the election petition.
The appellant challenged the High Court's decision, arguing that it did not have the power to summarily dismiss the petition on these grounds.
law: Under Section 87 of the Act, election petitions are to be tried, as nearly as may be, in accordance with the procedure applicable to the trial of suits under the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), 1908.
Under the Code of Civil Procedure, a suit that does not furnish a cause of action can be dismissed.
Section 83 of the Act mandates that an election petition must incorporate the material facts of the alleged corrupt practice.

The omission of a single material fact leads to an incomplete cause of action, and an election petition without the material facts relating to a corrupt practice is considered not to be an election petition at all.
application: The Supreme Court addressed the appellant's argument that Section 86 of the Act, which lists grounds for summary dismissal, does not include non-compliance with Section 83 (the requirement to state material facts).
However, the Court found that the power to dismiss comes from the Code of Civil Procedure, which is made applicable to election petitions by Section 87 of the Act.
The Court reasoned that the failure to incorporate the mandatory material facts as required by Section 83 results in the petition not disclosing a complete cause of action.
Since a suit without a cause of action can be dismissed under the CPC, an election petition with the same defect can also be summarily dismissed.

The Court concluded that there was "no escape from the conclusion" that an election petition can be summarily dismissed if it does not furnish a cause of action, in exercise of the powers under the Code of Civil Procedure.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, affirming that an election petition can be summarily dismissed if it fails to furnish the material facts and particulars of the alleged corrupt practices and, as a result, does not disclose a valid cause of action.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was right in holding that an election petition must be summarily dismissed when the material facts and particulars of the alleged corrupt practices are not furnished and the petition does not disclose a cause of action.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (the original election petitioner) contended that the High Court was wrong to dismiss the petition and made several submissions to assail the judgment, attempting to rely on charges of alleged corrupt practices.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the petition's pleadings were unsustainable and suffered from a lack of material facts.
The respondent contended that a proposed amendment by the petitioner was not merely clerical but would change the entire nature of the pleading, indicating it was made without proper consideration.
The respondent correctly urged that certain allegations, such as a request for 'instructions to the authorities', were misconceived and did not establish any legal obligation or corrupt practice.

cases.principle: A pleading alleging a corrupt practice that lacks essential particulars, such as the dates and details of a meeting, is a basic defect that cannot be cured by evidence and must be construed as disclosing no cause of action.

cases.case_name: Swnt w. llelkrislma & Anr. v. George Fernandez & Ors.
cases.principle: A pleading alleging a corrupt practice that lacks essential particulars, such as the dates and details of a meeting, is a basic defect that cannot be cured by evidence and must be construed as disclosing no cause of action.

cases.case_name: Udbav Singh v. ltadhav Rao Scindia Popatlal Mmd.lal Joshi & Ors.
cases.principle: A pleading alleging a corrupt practice that lacks essential particulars, such as the dates and details of a meeting, is a basic defect that cannot be cured by evidence and must be construed as disclosing no cause of action.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A pleading that alleges a corrupt practice but fails to provide essential particulars, such as the dates and details of a meeting, is considered a failure to incorporate material facts. This defect cannot be cured by evidence, and the pleading must be construed as disclosing no cause of action.
obiter: The possibility that witnesses could be procured for a convenient date or place if a pleading is vague is a reason why such pleadings should not be permitted.
A proposed amendment to a pleading that suffers from a lack of material facts may not be allowed.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The principle laid down is that the pleading in regard to matters where there is scope for ascribing an alleged corrupt practice to a returned candidate in the context of a meeting of which dates and particulars are not given would tantamount to failure to incorporate the essential particulars. No amount of evidence could cure the basic defect in the pleading and the pleading as it stood must be construed as one disclosing no cause of action.
legal_tests_applied: An election petition pleading must contain all material facts, and the omission of a single material fact would lead to an incomplete cause of action.
A pleading that fails to incorporate essential particulars, such as the dates and details of an alleged corrupt practice, must be construed as one disclosing no cause of action.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's pleading suffered from a lack of material facts and failed to incorporate the essential particulars of the alleged corrupt practice, specifically the dates and details of the meeting where it supposedly occurred.
The defect in the pleading was so basic that no amount of evidence could cure it, rendering the petition as one that disclosed no cause of action from the outset.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that the petition's pleading was not sustainable and suffered from a lack of material facts.
The High Court was correct in its conclusion that the defective pleading, which failed to provide essential particulars, disclosed no cause of action and therefore had to be dismissed.
policy_considerations: Strict pleading requirements are necessary to prevent abuse of the legal process, as without specific dates and particulars, there is a possibility that witnesses could be procured in the context of a meeting at a place or date convenient for adducing evidence.
Allowing a trial on a vague pleading would tend to prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial of the suit.
